title: Why Bhishma couldn't answer
hook: Draupadi asks the elders to their faces, and the greatest of them can't answer
carry: ahara shuddhi: as the food, so the mind

segments.voice: Yesterday Draupadi sent the messenger back with a question: whom had Yudhishthira lost first, himself or her? Asking what dharma requires is dharma too.

This part of the story is hard, and i'll tell it plainly and with care. Duhshasana goes to the women's rooms. Draupadi tries to get away, and he seizes her by the hair and drags her into the assembly. The telling says she's in a single garment, and in distress. Here's what stands out about her, in a hall full of men who have just watched her gambled away. She doesn't only cry out. She argues.
screen: `A HARD SCENE, TOLD WITH CARE.` → `DRAGGED INTO THE HALL.` → `SHE ARGUES.`

segments.voice: She looks at the elders and asks how they can sit and watch this. Where has the dharma of these kings gone? Then, plainly: was I won, or not? Answer it. Bhishma answers, and he is the greatest knower of dharma in that hall. The ways of dharma are subtle, he says. One who has lost himself can't stake what belongs to another. And yet a wife, as the custom of the time held, is under her husband's authority. Holding both, he says he can't settle it. Draupadi answers him sharply: Yudhishthira was called to play by skilled, crooked players, and had no skill himself. How was that a free choice? The epic leaves Bhishma's failure hanging. Hindu families tell a later story to answer it, one that isn't in the epic's own text. Years on, Bhishma lies dying on a bed of arrows, teaching dharma beautifully, and Draupadi laughs. Where was all this wisdom in the hall? And he tells her: back then i was living on Duryodhana's food, and it clouded my mind. The arrows have drained that blood, and now i see clearly. That story carries a real Hindu teaching: ahara shuddhi, purity of what we take in. The Chandogya Upanishad says that when what we take in is pure, the mind becomes pure. Families say it simply: as the food, so the mind. It means more than what's on the plate. It means how the food was earned, and whose table you owe.
screen: `WAS I WON, OR NOT?` · `BHISHMA: DHARMA IS SUBTLE.` · `WAS IT A FREE CHOICE?` · `ON THE BED OF ARROWS: IT WAS THE FOOD.` · then, large: `AS THE FOOD, SO THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Before your next meal or drink, pause for one breath and think about where it came from: who grew it, who earned it, who cooked it. Many Hindus say a short line before eating, like the Gita verse that begins brahmarpanam, offering the meal to God. If you pray, say it, or your own grace; if you don't, simply thank the hands behind the food.
Draupadi's question. She asked the elders to their faces, and Bhishma, who knew dharma best, called it subtle and couldn't answer.
Your line: ahara shuddhi: as the food, so the mind. In the story families tell, Bhishma's dinners cost him his voice. Go gently.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (Duhshasana brings Draupadi into the assembly; her appeal to the elders; Bhishma's answer that morality is subtle; Draupadi's reply that Yudhishthira was made to play by skilled and deceitful players)

Bhagavad Gita 4.24 (the brahmarpanam verse, widely said before meals)
